summary.text: Dendroclimatology works out past climates from trees, mainly by reading the properties of their yearly growth rings.
Rings grow wider in years good for growth and narrower in hard years, so a tree's rings hold a year-by-year record.
Matching ring patterns between samples lets scientists date them and extend records back using dead trees, old buildings and archaeological finds.

facts.label: Time span reached
facts.value: Local climates hundreds to thousands of years back

facts.label: Divergence problem began
facts.value: At some northern sites, rings and thermometers split since the 1950s

items.prompt: You cut a slice from an old pine and see a run of very thin rings in the middle. What do those rings most likely record?

options.label: Years when conditions made growth hard
Years when the tree was youngest
Years with unusually long summers
Years when the tree had more sunlight

items.explain: Rings are wider when conditions favor growth and narrower when times are difficult.

items.prompt: A researcher wants trees whose rings mostly track temperature rather than rainfall. Where on a mountain should she sample?

options.label: The lower edge of the forest
The upper treeline
A wet valley floor
Beside a busy logging road

items.explain: At the upper treeline, cold limits growth while rain is plentiful, so rings respond mostly to temperature; lower treelines respond more to rain.

items.prompt: A builder gives a dendroclimatologist old roof beams from a medieval house. Why can these beams help?

options.label: Old wood keeps a sample of the old air
Beams record the house's indoor heating
Their rings can be matched to other samples
Cut wood keeps growing rings after felling

items.explain: Matching ring patterns from sample to sample dates them, which lets records reach back using wood from buildings.

items.prompt: A gardener overwaters a house plant and it grows worse, not better. What problem for tree-ring reading does this illustrate?

options.label: Old trees grow more slowly than young ones
Sheep grazing can stunt a tree's growth
Rings are hard to date in the tropics
Growth may level off or reverse at extremes

items.explain: Ring width is usually assumed to rise steadily with a variable like moisture, but past a point the response can level off or turn the other way.

items.prompt: At some northern treeline sites, thermometers show strong warming since the 1950s but the tree rings do not. If you used only those rings to estimate earlier temperatures, what risk would you run?

options.label: Making the past look too cool
Making the past look too warm
Missing years with heavy frost
Dating rings a century early

items.explain: Using affected proxies can lead to overestimating past temperatures, which understates the current warming trend.

items.prompt: A team hopes to reconstruct past climate in a steamy rainforest using tree rings. Why might this fail?

options.label: Rainforest trees rot too fast to sample
The air there holds too much carbon dioxide
Trees there grow all year without clear rings
Tropical rings respond only to temperature

items.explain: In very wet tropical regions, trees generally grow year-round and do not show clear annual rings.
